verdicts.rewritten_summary: Context/Thomson Reuters (25 Sep 2024): Denmark's self-ID law (gender change without medical evaluation, in force since 2014) is credited by activists with cooling the trans debate; Denmark was the first country to recognise same-sex partnerships (1989) and ranks among the world's best for LGBTQ+ rights.

Outright country overview (updated 12 Mar 2026): same-sex couples may marry and adopt; discrimination on sexual orientation, gender identity, expression and sex characteristics is prohibited; trans people self-determine legal gender markers and non-binary people can choose an 'X' passport marker; Aug 2024 the government announced a plan to strengthen multi-parent (3-4 parent) families.

TV 2 Denmark (10 Sep 2024): the Supreme Court held it is not a human-rights violation for a trans inmate to serve in a men's prison department — the leading Danish authority on trans placement in custody.

Danish Institute for Human Rights LGBT+ barometer: 38% of homosexuals and bisexuals report differential treatment based on gender, sexual orientation or appearance; hate speech targeting sexual orientation, gender identity/expression or sex characteristics recurs annually.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2024 (covering 2023): UN Committee Against Torture 8th periodic review found some trans people, QTIBIPOCs and migrants report denial of access to spaces and services and threats; anti-trans discourse intensified as Parliament debated lowering the legal-gender-recognition age limit; committee urged psychosocial counselling and intersex remedy.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2025: in July a migrant trans woman was murdered in a hotel room in Copenhagen; 40% of LGBTI students aged 15-25 reported self-harm in the past year, two to three times their classmates' rate; Denmark signed a UN resolution against intersex discrimination (March).

WanderSafe 2026 Copenhagen guide: among the world's most LGBTQ+-welcoming cities — first country to recognise same-sex partnerships (1989), marriage 2012, gender self-declaration since 2014; Danish Equal Treatment Act covers sexual orientation and gender identity in employment/services; no conversion-therapy ban yet (bill revived Aug 2026).

F&M Global Barometers Denmark profile: gender-identity-based arbitrary arrest freedoms affirmed every year 2011-2024; workplace anti-discrimination laws have covered gender identity since 2015, with fair-housing gender-identity protection throughout the period.

HuffPost (5 Feb 2013): Guatemalan trans woman Fernanda Milan became the first transgender person granted asylum in Denmark — refused return over gender identity, citing police attacks and threats for her trans activism — an early marker of Denmark's asylum treatment of trans claimants.

Human Rights Watch (30 Aug 2024): documented the Constitutional Court challenge to sodomy-law remnants reaching only police and military officers (no equivalent for heterosexual acts), with HRW's amicus brief arguing equality/privacy violations. SUPERSEDED per resolved review: The 2024 constitutional review of the sodomy-law remnants is resolved: the current criminal code does not prohibit same-sex relations; still no anti-discrimination or marriage recognition.

verdicts.rewritten_summary: UPR database (Sexual Rights Initiative): the Dominican Republic accepted recommendations on intersex persons' rights and discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity — an accepted international-commitment record with no domestic implementation detail shown.

Time/Amnesty International (31 Mar 2019): TDOV conversation with two activists including Nairovi Castillo of the Dominican Republic, executive director of COTRAVETD (Community of Dominican Trans and Transvestite Sex Workers, co-founded 2004) — first-hand account of trans struggles in the country.

Washington Blade (1 Apr 2017): 300+ activists from Latin America and the Caribbean attended an LGBT/intersex political-engagement conference in Santo Domingo with Dominican government officials speaking — a marker of official-level engagement in 2017.

Washington Blade (27 Apr 2016): documents the backlash against openly gay US Ambassador James 'Wally' Brewster after his June 2015 presentation with his husband in Santo Domingo — framed as attacks on LGBT Dominicans, showing organised domestic opposition climate.

Washington Blade (3 Apr 2017): the openly gay US ambassador's departure left an advocacy void after two years of visible presence (spoke at Santo Domingo Pride, 3 Jul 2016) — trailing marker of the polarised climate his tenure exposed.

Cairo 52 country page (Algeria): NGOs document arrests within the LGBT+ community with little information on the trans identity of those arrested; no legal framework for gender-affirming healthcare — arts. 274/264 could be used against providers (de facto criminalisation); no legal gender-recognition route, so civil-status gender-marker changes are theoretically blocked.

UK Home Office CPIN 'Algeria: Sexual orientation and gender identity or expression' (26 Jul 2026, covering since May 2025): same-sex activity prohibited under Penal Code 1966 ('acts of homosexuality', Human Dignity Trust updated June 2026); internal relocation viable for gay males but lesbians and trans females face societal difficulties; refusals rarely certifiable as clearly unfounded — the current asylum-authority baseline.

Snopes fact-check (5 Aug 2024): Rating TRUE — Algeria prohibits medical and surgical gender-affirming care and being transgender; published while debunking the false Imane Khelif 'trans boxer' rumour, confirming the ban is real even though the rumour about the athlete was false.

US State Dept 2023 Country Reports (Algeria): law criminalised undefined 'homosexual acts' with 2 months' to 2 years' imprisonment plus fines; prison authorities separated vulnerable persons but LGBTQI+ detainees had no specific legal protections; civil society noted compounded discrimination for LGBTQI+ persons.

ILGA State-Sponsored Homophobia 2008: Algeria — male/male and female/female relations illegal under Penal Code (Ordinance 66-156 of 8 June 1966): 2 months' to 2 years' imprisonment and fines of 500-2000 Algerian dinars. Dated but the same Penal Code 1966 that the 2026 CPIN confirms is still in force.

Human Rights Watch (15 Oct 2020): after a 24 Jul 2020 raid on a private home in el-Kharoub, Constantine Province, police arrested 44 people (9 women, 35 men, mostly university students) over an alleged 'gay wedding'; on 3 Sep 2020 a court sentenced 2 to prison and 42 to suspended terms, using decorations and 'gay appearance' as evidence.

BBC/Arab Barometer (23 Jun 2019, 25,000 respondents across 10 countries + Palestinian territories): Algeria was the exception where fewer than 50% accepted a woman head of state; region-wide, 'not religious' identification rose from 8% to 13% since 2013 — social-conservatism context datum for the record.

Primicias (12 Jun 2024): President Noboa issued on 11 Jun 2024 the reglamento to the National Assembly's 12 Dec 2023 reforms of the Organic Law on Identity Management and Civil Data, streamlining civil-registry gender-marker changes — the operative procedure for legal gender recognition.

Outright country overview (updated 12 Mar 2026): same-sex marriage legalised in 2019 but same-sex couples barred from adoption by constitutional ban; legal gender recognition possible since 2016 (not available to under-18s); conversion practices involving torture are explicitly criminalised.

2008 Constitution of Ecuador (Georgetown/PDBA text): Article 11 principles bind the state to respect ethnic, national, social, generational and gender differences and sexual orientation and identity — the constitutional non-discrimination foundation for LGBTI rights in a secular, multinational state.

PinkNews (31 May 2018): the Constitutional Court ordered the Civil Registry to register the daughter of same-sex couple Helen Bicknell and Nicola Rothon (child Satya Amani Bicknell Rothon); lawyer Jose Luis Guerra said refusal violated the child's rights — a precedent ordering state recognition of same-sex families.

Cairo 52, 'Your Kind Is Not Welcome Here' (27 Nov 2023): analysis of Egypt's immigration law and case law plus 12 documented incidents (2018-2022) — Ministry of Interior holds broad powers to deny entry or deport anyone 'disturbing public order and morality', applied to travellers perceived as queer. Directly visitor-facing risk.

Cairo 52 (24 Jan 2024): Egypt's Economic Courts have moved from de-facto to EXPLICIT criminalisation by reading Penal Code provisions together with Art. 9(C) of the Anti-Sex Work Law 10/1961; Court of Cassation 1970s interpretations had already removed the financial-exchange requirement (habitual/multiple partners sufficed).

Cairo 52 (12 Dec 2024): a new Ministry of Interior directive to civil-registry heads nationwide closes the Civil Status Law 143/1994 loophole that let transgender Egyptians correct gender markers via governorate committees — legal gender recognition now actively being shut.

BBC investigation, 'How Egyptian police hunt LGBT people on dating apps': no explicit law against homosexuality, but the 'debauchery' (sex-work) law is used to criminalise the community; police run entrapment via apps with victims describing blackmail and arrests (names changed).

Bedayaa, '10 FAQs about LGBTIQs Situation in Egypt' (Feb 2023): documents rising arrests of homosexuals and trans people alongside coerced anal examinations, authorities turning a blind eye, and no anti-discrimination policy or law; covers detention conditions and the trans situation as a reference for SOGIESC work.

EIPR security documentation: police arrest patterns — first, entrapment of individuals, especially transgender women, through fake accounts on LGBTQ dating apps and websites; second, Ministry of Interior deportation of foreign nationals suspected of being gay or trans even without charges upheld; violations continue inside police stations.

Outright country overview (updated 12 Mar 2026): homosexuality not explicitly criminalised, yet vague public-morality and debauchery laws are routinely used for arrests carrying prison sentences; NO legal protection against discrimination on sexual orientation, gender identity, expression or sex characteristics.

TIMEP (6 Jan 2025): for Egypt's fourth UPR cycle — transgender and intersex Egyptians face discriminatory laws, policies and practices violating the right to health; barriers to equitable health services persist since the last UPR, with pervasive gender-identity and sexual-orientation discrimination in healthcare.

Human Rights Watch, 'In a Time of Torture: The Assault on Justice in Egypt's Crackdown on Homosexual Conduct' (29 Feb 2004): documents the Queen Boat-era crackdown — arbitrary arrests, dark cells and beatings over sexual orientation, with testimony from defendants — the landmark record of state violence against gay men in Egypt.

Outright country overview (updated 12 Mar 2026): Article 310(1) of the penal code criminalises 'homosexual conduct' with up to 7 years' imprisonment — inherited from the 1957 Ethiopian penal code and retained with an enhanced sentence in the first post-independence penal code (adopted 2015).

US State Dept 2023 Country Reports (Eritrea): Section 7 records that openly LGBTQI+ persons risked imprisonment and therefore did not participate in the political process; societal discrimination against LGBTQI+ persons continues alongside a law making no gender distinction for assault.

Asmarino relay of the US State Department 2011 human rights report on Eritrea: societal abuse and discrimination against gay men and lesbians occurred; the government labelled disloyal individuals 'gay, traitors, rapists, pedophiles'; the law criminalises consensual same-sex sexual activity.

UK Foreign Office 'Eritrea: Country of Concern' human rights report (© 2015): same-sex activity is a crime in Eritrea and there is no anti-discrimination legislation protecting lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender people; the UK raised these concerns bilaterally and via the EU.
